We justify our algorithm theoretically and empirically, demonstrating that our generative approach to representation learning avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression in cases where commonly used methods like DINO and LeJEPA fail. Moreover, we show our representation learning technique is scalable; expending more compute leads to predictably better latent tokenization. For the first time, we perform a careful analysis of the combined flop efficiency of tokenizer and generative model and demonstrate that our approach is a compute-optimal improvement over direct diffusion for pixel-space generation, obtaining an FID-50K of 2.18 with JiT-L. Applied to ImageNet and the text-to-image dataset GPIC, we show tokenizer encoder scaling laws for diffusability, where extrapolating our approach achieves representations in 7x fewer FLOPs than DINOv2 on ImageNet and 8x fewer FLOPs than WebSSL on GPIC.
n11d6aa34fa37: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can reveal disease-progression structure, while useful forecasting requires leakage-controlled discovery, censor-aware outcomes, and inspectable trajectory evidence. We developed a graph-enhanced framework in MIMIC-IV v3.1 that splits patients before graph construction, learns train-only consecutive-admission transitions, and freezes endpoint-specific branching-motif policies selected on validation data. The final catalog contained 99,527 motifs, and a time-aware Transformer retrieved at most 24 patient-compatible motifs per endpoint through endpoint-specific cross-attention. Across five training seeds, micro-AUPRC increased from 0.9330 to 0.9357, while event-time MAE decreased from 676.9 to 657.7 days (reduction 19.2 days; 95% paired patient-cluster bootstrap CI, 13.8-24.8). Timing effects were heterogeneous: MAE worsened for events within 730 days but improved by 58.9 days for events occurring after 730 days. In an exploratory internal temporal split, branch conditioning reduced conditional event-time MAE by 26.9 days (95% CI, 23.0-30.8) without evidence of better micro-AUPRC. Corrected survival evaluation over the supported 0-2,555-day interval did not establish macro C-index or integrated Brier score superiority over a matched history-only discrete-hazard model. A directed, degree-matched GNN repair substantially improved unseen-edge discovery, yet replacing GNN-derived scores within fixed motif identities did not improve downstream forecasting. These results position branching motifs as structured trajectory context whose main value is long-range timing support rather than uniformly stronger endpoint discrimination, survival prediction, or causal explanation.
n12d0c9a28f97: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website: https://hire-moma.github.io/
nc41d9c29d406: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory's own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen--Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared $100$-step schedule, HP-RLVR trains $1.21\times$, $1.46\times$, and $2.30\times$ faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, $43.2\%$ (4B) and $49.0\%$ (8B) of GRPO's gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.
na244b31c1366: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
nb3c06a4f2c8d: Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31\% and interior mean squared error by 47\%.
ndf22b5423dec: Foundation models have shown strong generalization across scientific domains, but their use in power systems remains largely task-specific. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TFM), TabPFN, can serve as a general-purpose neural solver for power grid steady-state analysis. We evaluate the TFM on three tasks: power flow (PF) prediction, N-k contingency screening (NCS), and voltage stability margin (VSM) prediction. We performed experiments on 118- and 2000-bus systems, comparing the TFM against task-specific neural baselines. Without retraining or fine-tuning, the TFM matches or outperforms the best task-specific model in several settings across the three tasks. For 118-bus PF prediction, a variant of the TFM achieves errors of $1\times 10^{-3}$ pu for voltage magnitudes and $0.30^\circ$ for voltage angles, outperforming all baselines. On unseen N-1 contingency and close-to-infeasible PF cases, the TFM is competitive with the DCPF approximation. For millions of unseen N-2 contingencies, the TFM achieves AUCs of 0.92 and 0.95 for branch and voltage violation screening, respectively. The TFM also attains accurate VSM prediction performance for the 2000-bus system with limited labelled data. The TFM attains strong results across the tested tasks despite pretraining without any power-system-specific dataset and requiring no fine-tuning step. These results offer a glimpse into the potential of pretrained TFMs as a neural solver for a range of power grid analysis tasks.
n8e88eb793eb6: Bias audits of multilingual language models usually compare a model's average stereotype score in English with its average in another language and read the difference as a difference in fairness. We ask how much of that difference is noise. Auditing ten open models in eight languages, we measure how far scores move when English test items are merely reworded, test every language shift item by item, and check that the test catches shifts we inject on purpose. In all 70 model-language pairs the stereotype score falls below its English level, and for Hindi, Korean and Swahili the drop clearly exceeds what rewording English produces; most of it comes from StereoSet items. Judging every translation, we find that imperfect ones drop more, but faithful translations alone drop nearly as much. Still, a lower average does not show that a model is fairer. An item's English score predicts its translated score far less well than its reworded score (correlation 0.23, 0.27 on faithful translations, vs. 0.48), while scores stay as far from neutral, models agree on translated items, and within Hindi or Spanish a translated item's score correlates with its own rewording at 0.84 and 0.82. The average cannot distinguish lower bias from a different pattern of item-level scores. We also document three common pipeline errors that silently erase bias signal, and release our code.
nc46bf8e11a0d: Brazilian Portuguese remains underserved by open-source language models, and the few that are safety-aligned rarely document what did not work or validate comparisons with statistical significance. We present Manacá-1B-Instruct-2, the second-generation post-training alignment of Manacá-1B (1.72B parameters, trained from scratch for PT-BR), with an SFT corpus of 291,223 examples. We document three DPO attempts, all negative, including a case where the training reward margin reaches 1.0 while free generation does not change at all, and show that safety came from a dedicated safety-SFT (LLM-jp AnswerCarefully style), refined over three iterations until closing the safety-helpfulness frontier. A controlled scan of the fraction of general data in the safety-SFT mix (10% to 60%) reveals a non-monotonic over-refusal curve with a knee point at 40-50%. The final model is compared against four external PT-BR models on the same items, with Wilson confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction: the lower bound of its safety interval (94.1%) lies above the upper bound of all four baselines. We also report a methodological finding for LLM-judge evaluation: on two of six safety items in MT-Bench-PT, the judge categorically refuses to assign a score regardless of the evaluated response, silently reducing the effective N of that category in every prior report of the project. We complement this with an n-gram decontamination check and a Chinchilla-anchored compute-budget table that attributes the gap in general capability to pre-training scale rather than alignment methodology. All code, raw data, logs, and scripts that produce every reported number are publicly released.
n9f526bd37e86: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot's kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website: https://humanoid-weight-diffusion.github.io/
ncd632fd1ae0e: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.
nee5c8c79e933: Post-training binds the competence of an LLM agent to the interface it was trained on. Semantics-preserving perturbations of that interface, such as renaming an action or changing the notation, leave the underlying task unchanged yet make the agent worse at it. Scoring each sample independently means interface randomization only broadens this dependence from a single interface to the training interface distribution, so out-of-distribution perturbations still degrade the agent. We propose Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR), a self-supervised objective that replaces action names with uninformative identifiers and presents each training sample under two interfaces in which equivalent actions are identified by construction. CIPR penalizes the KL divergence between the action distributions induced under the two interfaces, so the policy behaves consistently across them. We evaluate CIPR in both supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training, where it improves robustness. On agentic function calling, held-out interface perturbations reduce the accuracy of a post-trained agent by nearly 25%, and CIPR recovers 10.5% while leaving accuracy on the unchanged interface intact.
n93a52e9a6b25: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.
n8c88ea1d4575: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.
ne7aae1f823d3: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.
n6e6bdac3ac4c: Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions. However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control. Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. We introduce Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning. We construct Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO. The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively. Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld. Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL. We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.
n12905f1018ab: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.
n8dda165e88ea: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.
n22f39b0b6c93: Pretrained representations are increasingly used to share and reuse information from medical images without exposing the original scans, but it is unclear how much patient-specific information these representations retain. We investigate this question for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) by evaluating five frozen pretrained encoders spanning different architectures, pretraining objectives, and training domains on two longitudinal T1-weighted datasets, OASIS-2 and MIRIAD. Under an attacker model with access to released embeddings, the corresponding public encoder, and auxiliary MRI scans, we evaluate patient linkage and sensitive-attribute inference. Across the evaluated representations, we observe substantial subject-specific information: rank-1 patient linkage reaches up to 99\% on MIRIAD and exceeds 90\% on OASIS-2 for the highest-risk representation, despite the absence of an identification objective during encoder training. We further show that the released embeddings retain information about a demographic attribute, with recorded-sex prediction reaching balanced accuracy of 90.9\% on OASIS-2 and 95.5\% on MIRIAD. Overall, our results demonstrate that replacing raw brain MRI with learned embeddings does not, by itself, eliminate patient-linkage or attribute-inference risk, and is therefore insufficient on its own to establish anonymity.
n39d3d12ecaf9: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.
n469cd13c5ea1: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the student to rewrite its solution following the error. The resulting output, including the critique as privileged information, is scored by the teacher while the student uses the revision without the critique for training. On two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.
neba49e8e91f3: Relational deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning end-to-end predictive models over relational databases by representing them as temporal heterogeneous graphs. Recent advances based on graph neural networks and Transformers have achieved strong performance across diverse domains. However, the effectiveness of simpler relational baselines remains underexplored, making it difficult to assess how much architectural complexity is needed to achieve strong predictive performance. Motivated by the observation that predictive signals arise from target attributes, relational attributes, and historical labels, we revisit how effectively these signals can be exploited using simple propagation methods. We adapt fixed low-pass feature propagation to relational entity graphs and train an MLP for prediction. The resulting predictions are further refined using Correct-and-Smooth, a graph-based label propagation algorithm that incorporates historical labels over task-specific meta-graphs connecting target entities. Across classification and regression tasks on RelBench, an MLP trained on neighborhood-filtered features outperforms one using only target-entity features on most tasks and recovers a substantial portion of the performance of heterogeneous GNNs. Correct-and-Smooth provides further gains from historical labels, although applying it requires a separately constructed meta-graph because connections among target entities are not directly specified by the relational entity graph. Together, our studies revisit the effectiveness of established propagation methods as simple RDL baselines while identifying canonical meta-graph construction as a key challenge for effective label propagation.
n354b63967136: Opponent histories can mislead after behavioral shifts. SafeAdapt-Poker formulates budgeted adaptation under opponent shift as a dual-counterfactual sequential-control problem using only information available before each decision. At each decision the controller asks two distinct questions: what local downside a deviation from the frozen anchor would induce under matched legal continuations, and what future adaptation value would be lost by consuming part of the remaining deviation budget now. The first question is answered by a monotone strategic-risk model over deviation intensity; the second by a paired budget-state continuation model that prices current budget consumption. The controller selects among support-preserving candidate deviations by trading immediate adaptation value against these two quantities, a pathwise cumulative-KL ledger bounds total anchor-relative deviation, and a finite family of frozen controllers is screened on complete paired calibration sessions before held-out interaction. A finite-candidate perturbation bound shows that the allocation objective degrades continuously with continuation-value estimation error. Evaluation covers exact-game exploitation and safety, four opponent shifts, local-risk calibration, delayed-opportunity allocation, direct opportunity-value estimation, value-error robustness, factorial mechanism attribution, budget sensitivity, abstract-HUNL cross-play, and player/time-held-out public-history behavior. On exact Leduc the full controller attains a matched weak-pool gain of +0.0718 with a worst-opponent delta of -0.0126, raises delayed-opportunity capture from 0.6318 under myopic allocation to 0.7841 under the same session budget, and reaches +42.7 mbb/hand in abstract-HUNL cross-play; the retained public-history screen reports 0.5820 action accuracy and 0.9277 log loss versus 0.5039 and 0.9778 for a public prior.
n0d86fa32054e: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.
ncdff4cad8bbe: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
n438892f2dfb9: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.
nbed57cb9b9c6: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents' research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can combine evidence and implementations from different research directions to guide their agents' subsequent experiments. However, poor experimental results can leave unclear whether to revise a hypothesis or its implementation, while overall program scores can hide components useful to other agents. To address these challenges, we introduce SwarmRSI, a framework that evolves scientific agent swarms for recursive self-improvement. We devise Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation to refine hypotheses and their implementations using experimental feedback from other agents. We also propose Complementary Swarm Recombination to reuse retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, allowing partial results to support new research. Recursive Swarm Evolution integrates both mechanisms into a feedback loop, using new experimental evidence to guide subsequent research. Experiments on OpenProblems, NatureBench and MLE-Bench Lite demonstrate SwarmRSI's state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Further evaluations show that accumulated research experience improves performance on held-out tasks. Biologists also reproduce its programs for follow-up biological analyses.
n464c4661f650: We study classification dynamics under small initialization and identify a pronounced non-monotone behavior of accuracy that we call the accuracy well: accuracy rises rapidly early in training, subsequently drops, and only much later recovers. We observe this phenomenon in deep linear networks, fully connected ReLU networks on MNIST, deep convolutional networks on CIFAR-10, and controlled synthetic tasks, across different losses and optimizers and in both training and test accuracy. We propose a three-stage explanation in terms of target-driven organization, a degeneracy bottleneck, and subsequent recruitment and recovery. We develop a rigorous theory of these dynamics for shallow and deep linear networks, showing in particular that high accuracy can emerge while the predictor and the change in loss remain asymptotically vanishing, before continued optimization causes accuracy to deteriorate. For a simple synthetic classification task, we prove an extreme instance in which accuracy asymptotically rises to 100%, collapses to 0, and later recovers permanently to 100%. Our results show that classification accuracy can reveal aspects of learning dynamics that are not captured by the training loss alone.
n0aa2c5222076: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. We use the corpus frequencies to weight together the LM's own unembeddings of the next tokens most often following the current n-gram history. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.
ndfbde7d233d3: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.
n6ed2ffb255c7: Today's agentic systems are typically designed, built, and deployed by single developers with full control over all participating agents. While this simplifies development, it limits the potential scale of agentic systems. We study multi-developer agentic systems (MDAs) which enable developers to collaboratively build agentic systems to push frontier capability beyond what any individual developer could achieve alone. We construct empirical and theoretical models of developers to compare MDAs with single-developer agentic systems (SDAs). On GAIA, a general assistant benchmark, a population of specialized developers whose individual agents do not exceed 35% accuracy reaches 70% when their agents are combined in an MDA. This MDA performs 12 percentage points above the median general-purpose SDA built with several times each specialist's development budget. Our theoretical models show how MDAs can incentivize specialization and encourage more efficient use of aggregated developer resources. Put together, our results make a preliminary case for MDAs as a new scaling axis by enabling developers with diverse capabilities and resources to advance agentic AI collaboratively.
nb6feed0df566: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.
nfb10d2316208: Generative super-resolution (SR) can recover sharp detail in computed tomography (CT) images from severely downsampled observations, but the missing high-frequency content is not uniquely determined by the low-resolution input. Consequently, visually plausible reconstructions may contain anatomically unsupported vascular detail, such as missing, spurious, or incorrectly connected vessels. To overcome this challenge, we introduce VascuSR, an iterative anatomy-aware diffusion framework that combines image reconstruction with explicit 3D vascular guidance. First, to provide richer anatomical guidance, we use an explicit 3D vascular representation that captures structural information beyond individual slices. This representation also simplifies vascular refinement by allowing a lightweight 3D generative refiner to focus on vascular structure rather than complex CT appearance. Second, to guide slice-wise SR, a lightweight anatomy controller injects the refined structure into the diffusion decoder, while iterative feedback updates this guidance from each new SR volume. On re-annotated MSD Task08 and HVM datasets, VascuSR outperforms interpolation and learning-based SR baselines in segmentation accuracy (Dice and clDice) and 3D vascular structure (connectivity and mean centerline distance), while maintaining image quality comparable to its SR backbone. Compared with learning-based baselines, VascuSR reduces class-averaged connected-component counts by over 20% on both datasets and mean centerline distance by over 10% on MSD.
n3aaebc8ca044: Pairwise comparison data are a standard supervision signal in preference learning, but disagreement in such data can reflect stable latent heterogeneity, ephemeral stochasticity, or non-binary responses hidden by a forced-choice interface. We study which of these semantic distinctions are identifiable from the feedback channel itself. We introduce a nonparametric latent semantic model with three querywise quantities: aggregate directional preference $μ_q$, persistent disagreement $τ_q$, and non-binary mass $α_q$. Under the anonymous binary channel, we prove an exact semantic fiber theorem: $μ_q$ is point-identified, whereas $(τ_q, α_q)$ vary over an explicit feasible region compatible with the same binary law. Same-annotator repeats identify $τ_q$ through a covariance identity, abstention-enabled feedback identifies $α_q$ directly, and together they point-identify the full semantic triple. We also derive finite-sample estimators, nonasymptotic concentration bounds, and semantics-aware action-recovery guarantees, and validate the theory on theorem-matched synthetic data.
n014f193bc399: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.
n86612f1b662e: Crack-path instabilities in solids are typically associated with high propagation velocities. In contrast, we show that nanoparticle-filled elastomers exhibit a sideways crack-path instability that is amplified as the pulling velocity decreases and nearly vanishes at high pulling velocities. The sideways deviation amplitude decreases logarithmically with increasing pulling velocity and scales as the square root of the filler fraction. Large deviations develop at low mean crack velocities and are associated with effective fracture energies up to two orders of magnitude lower. These findings are consistent with subcritical rupture kinetics and suggest that the deviation amplitude is limited by the elasto-adhesive length.
n21ab74b63dcf: We investigate the statistical properties and ergodic behavior of the absolute area below the trajectory of a particle subject to stochastic resetting and moving according to a scaled Brownian motion with exponent $β$. We compare the contributions to the absolute area from the waiting times between resets and the backward recurrence time. Using the renewal formalism we derive the lower-order moments of the absolute area under both Poissonian and heavy-tailed power-law resetting waiting time distributions with exponent $α$. For Poissonian resetting, stochastic interruption suppresses fluctuations, driving the area to be ergodic, regardless of the value of $β$. In contrast, power-law resetting yields a rich spectrum of ergodic regimes. For $0 < α< 1$, the system displays weak ergodicity breaking and the maximum contribution dominates the area accumulated during the waiting times. For $1+β< α< 2$, we unveil an ergodic transition exclusive to the subdiffusive regime at $α=1+β$, where ergodicity is restored. These results clarify the subtle interplay between anomalous diffusion and power-law waiting times between resettings. Our results are tested by numerical simulations exhibiting an excellent agreement.
n2c775a09e498: Active flows are often confined by soft, deformable boundaries that they can push against, reshape, and in turn get reorganized by. Motivated by this interplay, we combine theory and numerical simulations to analyze the morphodynamics of an elastic vesicle enclosing a dilute suspension of extensile active particles. We model the two-dimensional vesicle as a weakly extensible elastic ring with bending rigidity, immersed in a Stokesian fluid, and describe the confined active suspension using a kinetic theory. The vesicle and the suspension are coupled hydrodynamically, through the kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the interface, and energetically, through a single alignment interaction that simultaneously aligns active particles with the membrane and the membrane with the particles. We show that this interaction reduces to a weak-anchoring boundary condition familiar from passive liquid crystals and derive a closed-form quiescent equilibrium state in which the nematic order in the suspension organizes into a vortex with a +1 defect core. A stability analysis of this state predicts an ordered hierarchy of activity thresholds at which successive shape modes of the vesicle are destabilized, as well as a purely passive, anchoring-driven instability of floppy vesicles. Nonlinear simulations, performed with a volume-conserving immersed boundary method, reveal that each threshold crossing gives rise to a distinct emergent state: a static spindle with boundary-pinned defects, a rotor that tank treads against its own rotation, a fluctuating spinner, and a turbulent state in which the vesicle acts as a self-stirring compartment. Beyond demonstrating how boundary deformability sculpts, and is sculpted by, confined active matter, our results open the door to study hydrodynamic interactions between such active vesicles and to use membrane fluctuations as a probe of activity of suspensions.
n9a0a81eac81c: Recent photoluminescence experiments in twisted MoTe$_2$ have reported signatures of anyons binding to trapped trions. The measured binding energies near the fractional Chern insulators at fillings of $ν=-2/3$ and $-3/5$ have a ratio close to the fractional-charge ratio $5/3$, even though such scaling is not generally guaranteed for the expected short-range trion-anyon interaction. We model the trapped trion as a fixed impurity, and investigate anyon-impurity binding using a lowest-Landau-level model with exact diagonalization and Jain wavefunctions. Surprisingly, we find that the anyon-impurity binding energy ratio between $ν=-2/3$ and $-3/5$ is close to $5/3$ for either short- or long-ranged impurity-electron interactions. However, the ratio departs strongly from the charge ratio at intermediate ranges or different Jain states. Remarkably, we also uncover "wrong-sign" binding, whereby both quasiholes and quasiparticles can bind to either sign of a short-range impurity potential by selecting orbital channels with favorable local density oscillations. Our findings show that localized excitons or trions can be used to probe the internal density profile of anyons.
n54cc337b46c0: The resetting of stochastic processes has become a key mechanism appearing in many research fields, such as searching for a target, the transmission control protocol, biology, chemistry, finance, insurance, etc., with the main interest concerning the first passage time (FPT) by the process under resetting. In this paper, we focus on the exit time $\mathcal{T}_L$ from the interval $(-L, L)$ of Lévy flights (LF) under resetting, but we also consider spectrally negative Lévy processes (SNLP). As the main result, we find the asymptotics of the mean first passage time (MFPT) as $L$ tends to $+ \infty$. For LF with $α\in (0, 2)$, the scaling behaves as $L^α$ regardless of the reset rate and the asymmetry of the initial condition, a behaviour completely different from that for the known case of Brownian Motion ($α=2$). For the symmetric $α$-stable case with $α\in (0, 2)$, we also found that taking $r \to \infty$ with fixed $L$ yields a finite MFPT, which therefore may be used as a valid approximation. For completely asymmetric stable processes, we show that the scaling is very different from that for LF, and point out a method to obtain the exact distribution of FPT under resetting. The analytical calculations are verified by numerical simulations of the processes under resetting.
n94ebeab48830: We demonstrate control between level repulsion and level attraction of photon-magnon coupling spectra in a chiral microwave-photon resonator loaded with a 2 mm YIG sphere. By systematically varying the coupling mode volume via the YIG position and the dc-field orientation, we tune the ratio between coherent and dissipative coupling strengths, $J/Γ$, and thereby switch between level repulsion and level attraction in the hybrid spectra. Full-wave electromagnetic and magnetization-dynamics simulations reveal multiple photon-magnon hybrid modes with distinct spatial overlap factors, which quantitatively account for gap sizes and their angular dependence. Strong nonreciprocity appears near $J/Γ\approx 1$, yielding 28.6 dB isolation ratio in agreement with a unified single-bath input-output model and full-wave simulations. Angular dependence of spectral characterization confirms a picture of the chirality-selection rule and our method of geometric tuning might be useful for considering reconfigurable on-chip isolators.
nb6e191cfd019: Binary active systems offer a minimal platform for understanding how component heterogeneity organizes non-equilibrium structures. Here we show that in a binary Quincke system driven by a periodic square-wave electric field, a dynamic square lattice in which small particles occupy the lattice-cell centers which are surrounded by large particles emerges spontaneously. Particle-resolved trajectories reveal that the size separation arises from the mobility difference of large particles and small particles. Increasing the driving frequency reduces the single-cycle path lengths of both species and simultaneously decreases the lattice constant. These results show how size-dependent activity,density redistribution, and periodic forcing cooperate to generate tunable complex active patterns.
n5e6b1a661f0b: We investigate the role of different correlation functions in reconstructing the phase diagram of the spin-1 bilinear-biquadratic chain, parametrized by the angle $θ$ between the bilinear and biquadratic couplings, using our previously developed label-free machine-learning pipeline \cite{Ming21, Ming23}, in which an autoencoder compresses iDMRG correlation matrices into latent features and K-means clustering with silhouette analysis groups them into phases. Without any prior labels, the scheme reveals four natural phases, the Haldane, dimerized, critical trimerized, and ferromagnetic phases, and accurately locates the Takhtajan-Babujian ($θ=-π/4$), $SU(3)$-symmetric Uimin-Lai-Sutherland ($θ=π/4$), and Ferro-Dimer ($θ=5π/4$) transition points; a shallow supervised refinement further sharpens the phase boundaries. We find that different correlation functions play fundamentally different roles in phase identification. The $SU(3)$-symmetric correlation alone selects a four-cluster partition that can be associated with the four phases, whereas the spin-spin and dimer-dimer correlations must be combined to recover the complete phase diagram. In contrast, the trimer-trimer correlation behaves as a marginal correlation: it is insufficient for phase identification by itself but improves the precision of the predicted phase boundaries when combined with the other correlations. Furthermore, the latent representations and silhouette values reveal signatures that we relate to the $θ$ dependence of the correlations within each phase and, tentatively, to the underlying renormalization-group structure. These results demonstrate that machine learning can not only identify quantum phases but also uncover the physical information encoded in different correlation functions.
n3782b4d8041e: The zero modes of the Aharonov-Casher Hamiltonian form an exactly flat, vortexable Chern band in any nonuniform magnetic field, analogous to the lowest Landau level. We ask which local Hamiltonians host exactly flat higher-vortexable bands. For a scalar Hamiltonian, an exactly flat first-vortexable band requires a mass proportional to the local field; the Dirac analogue has the same structure. For periodic Bernal bilayer graphene with nonzero mean flux, the exact zero-mode pair is genuinely first-vortexable if and only if the interlayer hopping has nonzero mean; zero-mean hopping instead gives a decomposable pair. Multiorbital models yield exact higher-vortexable chains to arbitrary order, while remaining first order in momentum.
n61b688c72962: A comprehensive understanding of complex transition-metal oxides is key to designing next-generation spintronic materials with tailored magnetic and transport functionalities. We investigate the interplay among structural disorder, frustrated magnetism, and localized charge transport in the 3d-4d hybrid double perovskite Sr2FeRuO6. The compound adopts a monoclinic structure with significant B-site antisite disorder that drives its unconventional behavior. Magnetic measurements uncover a robust Griffiths phase extending well above the ordering temperature, evidencing stable short-range ferromagnetic clusters within a disordered matrix. Electrical transport remains strongly localized, transitioning from small-polaron hopping at high temperatures to variable-range hopping at intermediate temperatures. These results position Sr2FeRuO6 as a representative 3d-4d hybrid system in which quenched disorder stabilizes spin inhomogeneity, while polaronic and hopping transport are also observed.
ne8cb0e5b6f13: Onsager solved the two-dimensional Ising model in zero field, but no solution is known in a magnetic field. We prove that in any dimension $d\ge2$, at every fixed dimensionless field outside a countable set, the free energy obeys no algebraic differential equation in the coupling, even locally. The obstruction arises from droplet geometry: the maximal droplet volume grows as the $d/(d-1)$ power of its boundary size, while an integer band in the pressure coefficients protects the extremal contributions against cancellation. Our result excludes Onsager-type solutions and closed forms in elliptic, hypergeometric, or Painlevé functions of the coupling at these fields.
n40e5d19d95bf: Synthetic active surfaces are usually designed to attain a prescribed static configuration, with dynamic shape changes typically requiring modulation of the actuation. We show that thin active shells can instead sustain dynamic morphing under a steady stimulus by harnessing flutter instability. We focus on polyelectrolyte hydrogel shells immersed in a viscous fluid and subjected to a constant and uniform electric field, and specialize the non-Euclidean framework for thin structures to account for field-induced activity through a spontaneous curvature evolving in time with the system configuration. Examining elliptic plates and cylindrical shells as test cases, we integrate linear stability analyses with nonlinear simulations to first locate the onset of flutter and then unveil the resulting dynamics, characterized by thrust-generating shape changes. In all cases, the emergent behavior stems from the interplay between active reconfiguration and elasticity in the fluid environment. For plates, the problem is purely flexural in the linear regime, while the competition between bending and stretching becomes crucial in selecting the ensuing shapes and swimming trajectories at large deformations. Conversely, for cylindrical shells bending and stretching are coupled at all levels, with the latter becoming essential to sustain flutter. Experiments on millimeter-sized hydrogel plates provide tangible support for our theoretical findings through shape reconstructions performed by combining digital image correlation with optical stereo microscopy. Flutter thus offers a route to untethered soft robotic and microfluidic devices based on active shells and operating under a stimulus carrying neither an intrinsic frequency nor a characteristic length scale.
na4f7d049880a: Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.
nc59b17e1ee78: Advances in polymer synthesis and computational modeling are expanding the block-copolymer architecture space accessible for phase-behavior design. Machine learning can accelerate this exploration, yet a common representation capable of learning across diverse chain topologies remains lacking. Here, we present a graph neural network (GNN) representation of acyclic AB multiblock architectures, tested by random-phase approximation (RPA) instability prediction. Each chain is represented as a graph, enabling a common model to learn across diverse topologies. This representation, which organizes RPA-related information, retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks and demonstrates its potential for reuse across tasks through transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction. By effectively linking block-copolymer chain architecture to field-theoretic response, this graph representation not only reconstructs stability-limit curves but also provides a practical route for future self-consistent field theory exploration of ordered phase space across complex topologies.
n9dbd80e837f3: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.
n88c81ed16687: Altermagnetism gives rise to momentum-dependent spin splitting without net magnetization. Here, we use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate bulk $α$-MnTe single crystals cleaved along the $(1\bar{1}00)$ plane - an orientation that preserves the compensated magnetic symmetry at the surface and substantially reduces surface effects and $k_z$ broadening. We resolve the three-dimensional bulk band structure with markedly enhanced spectral clarity. The $d$-wave band splitting, driven by the altermagnetic order and spin-orbit coupling in the $\mathbfΓ-\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{M}$ nodal plane, shows a perfect match to theoretical predictions. We further establish that the valence-band maximum occurs near the $\mathbf{A}$ point, identifying the corresponding hole pockets as the states governing the transport properties. Spatially resolved measurements reveal systematic variations of the band dispersion along $\mathbfΓ-\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{L}$, associated with different pinning of the Néel vector at the surface. Our results establish a surface-sensitive route to resolving the bulk altermagnetic electronic structure of MnTe and provide direct spectroscopic evidence for Néel-vector-dependent band splitting.
nba836e3c0477: Layer polarization provides a means of tuning the competition between interlayer and intralayer pairing in bilayer nickelates. Using ground-state constrained-path quantum Monte Carlo, we study interlayer $s^{\pm}$ and intralayer $d$ pairing in a bilayer two-orbital Hubbard model with a layer potential-energy difference $\varepsilon$ representing an effective perpendicular electric field. Within the parameter range studied, increasing $\varepsilon$ generally enhances the finite-size pairing vertex contribution $V_d$ and reduces $V_{s^{\pm}}$, shifting the relative pairing preference toward the $d$-wave channel. Increasing the onsite repulsion enhances both vertex contributions, more strongly in the $d$-wave channel, whereas increasing the crystal-field splitting reduces both and makes $s^{\pm}$ pairing relatively more competitive. Hund's coupling increases the relative competitiveness of $s^{\pm}$ pairing at weak bias, while enhancing the relative strength of $d$-wave pairing at large bias. The bias primarily redistributes charge between layers within each orbital sector, accompanied by an increase in the antiferromagnetic spin structure factor. Hund's coupling also enhances local interorbital parallel-spin correlations. These observations suggest possible connections between charge redistribution, magnetic correlations, and pairing competition, offering insight into how layer polarization and multiorbital interactions influence the relative pairing tendencies in the bilayer nickelate model.
n4bc9ee38334a: The lower-symmetry $Am2m$ structure was recently proposed as the intrinsic ambient-pressure phase of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction, whereas earlier studies investigated its properties assuming the commonly accepted $Amam$ structure. Here, we reexamine the crystal structure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ and the spin configuration of spin-density-wave (SDW) state via $^{139}$La nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR). The observation of two distinct La(2) sites in the NQR spectra is naturally accounted for by the $Am2m$ structure without any special assumptions, whereas it cannot be reconciled within the $Amam$ framework. Within the $Am2m$ framework, we reanalyze the spin configuration of the SDW phase and identify it as a large-tiny spin-stripe structure, arising naturally from two inequivalent Ni sites with large and tiny magnetic moments. These results establish the itinerant nature of the SDW order at ambient pressure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, providing a basis for understanding its relationship to the emergence of high-$T_c$ superconductivity under high pressure.
na7bef77d13fa: Extracting the London penetration depth, $λ(T)$, from the measured magnetic susceptibility, $χ(T)$, of a superconducting platelet in a perpendicular magnetic field requires knowing the function $χ(λ)$ computed for the actual sample geometry. Thin films are increasingly important in quantum computing and superconducting electronics, most of which operate at ultra-low excitation fields in the vortex-free regime. Understanding their electromagnetic response in the Meissner--London (finite-$λ$, no vortices) state is therefore essential for extracting intrinsic properties such as the London penetration depth and superfluid phase stiffness. While numerous prior works have addressed different aspects of this problem, here we focus on providing an analytical semi-empirical representation of $χ(λ)$ based on the 2D sheet-current model and establishing the limits of its applicability using two independent full 3D numerical solutions: finite-element modeling and a volume-current integral equation. As a result, we provide $χ(λ)$ for a disc of radius $a$ and thickness $d$ in closed form, valid for all $λ$ and for aspect ratios $δ\equiv d/(2a)\le0.05$, and accurate to $0.1\%$. The two-dimensional sheet description with Pearl length $Λ=2λ^2/d$ is adequate for $δ\lesssim10^{-4}$ and $λ\gtrsim 4d$. Thicker films require the full closed form, which includes the three-dimensional corrections. Using the same numerical analysis, we provide an empirical formula that maps rectangular samples---the geometry most commonly used in experiments---onto a disc with an ``effective radius'' for subsequent calculation of $χ(λ)$, and formulate a complete calibration protocol for whole-sample susceptibility measurements.
ne311bbf183ad: Magnetic proximity effects in transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD)/2D-magnet heterostructures are often described in terms of the magnetization of the interfacial magnetic layer. Here, we show that this picture is sufficient to describe the neutral-exciton valley splitting of the TMD, but incomplete for its hole-doped electronic structure. We study a gate-tunable van der Waals heterostructure composed of monolayer WSe$_2$ in direct contact with trilayer CrI$_3$. By combining spatially and helicity-resolved reflection-contrast spectroscopy with magnetic circular dichroism, we identify two distinct magnetic domains in the trilayer CrI$_3$: one with purely antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling and one with a mixed antiferromagnetic (AFM)/ferromagnetic~(FM) coupling. In both domains, the sign of the neutral-exciton valley splitting of WSe$_2$ switches with the magnetization reversal of the adjacent CrI$_3$ layer. In contrast, helicity-resolved positive-trion spectroscopy of WSe$_2$ reveals a qualitatively different response. While the AFM domain shows a strongly helicity-selective trion resonance, the mixed AFM/FM domain exhibits trion resonances in both helicities. This behavior disappears when all CrI$_3$ layers are aligned in a parallel magnetization direction. Our results demonstrate that charged excitons are sensitive to the full layer-resolved magnetic sequence of the adjacent 2D-magnet, revealing magnetic proximity beyond the interface.
n09a1c75c13fe: Recent progress in programmable quantum simulators motivates exact benchmarks for nonequilibrium dynamics in topological quantum matter. We study the Kitaev honeycomb model driven through its critical regions by a linear ramp of the bond coupling $J_z$ over a ramp time $τ$, comparing zigzag and armchair ribbons with fully periodic tubes. The production of excitations exhibits a geometry-dependent finite-size crossover controlled by $N_2/\sqrtτ$, the ratio of the ribbon width to the Kibble--Zurek length. Periodic tubes obey the expected critical-line Kibble--Zurek scaling and serve as the boundary-free benchmark. Zigzag ribbons follow the same scaling until defect production is exponentially suppressed by a finite-width algebraic gap floor associated with the formation of Majorana edge modes, whose occupation is pinned by inversion parity. Armchair ribbons instead support transient Majorana edge modes with exponentially small gaps, producing width-parity-dependent defect plateaus: exactly one defect per unit length for odd widths and an approximate, transient plateau near one half for even widths. The quench-generated entanglement entropy and fermionic logarithmic negativity inherit the same geometry-dependent structure, and the negativity further distinguishes the coherence-borne entanglement of the Kibble--Zurek regime from the population-borne entanglement of the edge-mode plateaus. These results identify boundary Majorana modes as the mechanism controlling departures from ideal Kibble--Zurek dynamics and provide geometry-resolved benchmarks for programmable simulations of topological matter.
n0fc04795b8cf: Interlayer excitons (IXs) in transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers possess unique dipolar properties, providing a path for exploring correlated many-body phases, electrically tunable dipole-dipole interactions, and long-range exciton transport. However, the large electron-hole separation underlying their dipolar character also results in a significantly reduced oscillator strength, limiting their direct optical interaction with light, and thus the direct probing of their dynamics and many-body interactions. Here, we show that by using Purcell engineering of critical coupling, a weak interlayer transition can absorb as strongly as the dominant intralayer transition, despite its much smaller intrinsic oscillator strength. Using this approach, in an open cavity architecture we demonstrate an order of magnitude IX absorption modulation in bilayer and trilayer MoS2, with doubling of the IX to A-exciton interaction strength weight from ~23% to ~53%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a tailored closed cavity architecture, the IX enhancement can reach beyond an order of magnitude, from ~5% to ~83% excitonic absorption, enabling IX absorption similar to intralayer excitons.
